🇧🇷 Brazil may be turning into one of the most interesting macro elections of the year. Lula now leads Flávio Bolsonaro by just 46% to 45% in a runoff in the latest BTG/Nexus poll.

➡️ Bolsonaro has chosen to attack Lula on debt, interest rates and the cost of capital, probably the most sensitive economic issue in Brazil today. Public debt is approaching 100% of GDP under international metrics and the overall deficit remains high. The more investors question the fiscal trajectory, the higher the risk premium they demand. The higher rates stay, the larger the government’s interest bill becomes. The larger that bill becomes, the more debt keeps rising. Therefore the issue remains the inability to sustainably bring down the country’s cost of funding.

📉 Bolsonaro also now has very concrete examples to support that narrative. Casas Bahia recently filed for bankruptcy protection with more than 17 billion reais of debt while Braskem is restructuring close to $11 billion. These situations cannot be explained solely by Lula’s fiscal policy but electorally the message is extremely effective.

🤷‍♂️ Meanwhile, Bolsonaro is also trying to make his economic platform more credible by bringing in figures linked to the former Guedes team and putting debt stabilization at the center of his message. If he keeps gaining in the polls while presenting a genuinely credible fiscal program, markets could quickly start pricing a stronger real, lower long-term yields and a rerating of domestic equities that are highly sensitive to the cost of capital. Conversely, if Lula starts making more fiscal concessions to secure reelection, the risk premium could remain elevated.

The Brazilian election is clearly starting to become a referendum on the cost of money.

MISLEADING MATH

Just so everyone understands the sleight of hand here:

Van Nieuwerburgh, the source cited in this chart, actually estimated AI infrastructure investment at 2.8% of GDP, not 3.6%.

His math: $8.2T of investment over 8 years = ~$1.025T/year. He assumes nominal GDP grows 5% annually while the buildout happens. That gets him to 2.8%.

So how did Steve get 3.6%?

Even if you make the absurd assumption that nominal GDP doesn't grow at all from today's $32.5T:

$1.025T / $32.5T = 3.15%

Still not 3.6%.

To get 3.6%, you either need a GDP denominator smaller than the economy is today, or roughly $1.2T more AI investment over 8 years than the source you're citing assumes.

And then that 3.6% gets compared with railroad investment averaged over 20 years 🤡 

I'm sure there will be plenty of AI malinvestment. The actual numbers are interesting enough. 

So why juice them?

Can a sufficiently powerful quantum computer forge the signatures used to authorize Bitcoin and Ethereum transactions? What would it take to upgrade both networks before that happens?

In this new lecture, Stanford cryptographer @danboneh explores why blockchains may turn to signatures built from hash functions. He also presents new research on threshold signing.

The talk ends with the questions Bitcoin still has to answer, including whether post-quantum signatures will require larger blocks, what happens to abandoned coins, and how someone such as Satoshi could prove ownership after Bitcoin’s current signatures have been retired.
